lessons.title: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost
lessons.objective: Explain scarcity, choice and opportunity cost, and rank competing wants with a scale of preference.

content.heading: The economic problem
paragraphs: Economics begins with a mismatch: human wants are unlimited, but the resources used to satisfy them are limited. That gap is scarcity, and it forces everyone — households, firms and governments — to choose.
bullets: Scarcity means resources are insufficient to satisfy every want at once. It is not the same as shortage, which is temporary.
Because resources are scarce, choosing one use means giving up another.
A scale of preference ranks wants in order of importance, so limited income goes to the most pressing wants first.
Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone — not the money paid.

content.heading: How societies answer three questions
paragraphs: Every economy must decide what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. The way it answers those questions defines its economic system.
bullets: Free enterprise (capitalist): private individuals own the factors of production and prices coordinate most decisions.
Centrally planned (socialist): the government owns and directs resources through a plan.
Mixed economy: markets and government both allocate resources. Nigeria is a mixed economy — private firms dominate production while government regulates and provides public goods.
The production possibility frontier shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce; a point inside the curve is inefficient.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Opportunity cost is the alternative you gave up, not the naira you spent. If you spend N2,000 on data instead of a textbook, the opportunity cost is the textbook.

content.problem: A student has N2,000. She ranks a textbook first, a data bundle second and a cinema ticket third. She buys the textbook. What is her opportunity cost?

steps.reason: Opportunity cost is measured against what was actually chosen.
steps.predictPrompt: Which want came next on her scale of preference?

steps.reason: Only the highest-ranked forgone option counts, not every option she skipped.
steps.result: The data bundle is the next best alternative.

steps.reason: The N2,000 is the money cost; it is not the forgone alternative.
steps.result: Opportunity cost = the data bundle she did not buy.

content.question: Nigeria is usually described as a mixed economy. Name one decision left mainly to markets and one left mainly to government, then explain why scarcity makes the choice necessary.
hints: Markets decide most prices and what private firms produce; government provides defence, roads and regulates utilities.
Scarcity means not every want can be met, so someone must decide which wants come first.
A strong answer links the two sectors to the three questions — what, how and for whom — and names opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Demand, Supply and Equilibrium
lessons.objective: Apply the laws of demand and supply, distinguish shifts from movements, and solve for equilibrium price and quantity.

content.heading: Demand and its determinants
paragraphs: The law of demand says that, all else equal, quantity demanded falls as price rises. The demand curve therefore slopes downward.
bullets: A change in the good’s own price moves you along the demand curve — a change in quantity demanded.
A change in income, tastes, population, expectations or the price of a related good shifts the whole curve — a change in demand.
Normal goods: demand rises with income. Inferior goods: demand falls as income rises.
Types of demand: complementary (used together), competitive (substitutes), composite (one good, many uses), derived (demand for a factor from demand for its product).

content.heading: Supply and equilibrium
paragraphs: The law of supply says quantity supplied rises with price, so the supply curve slopes upward. Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
bullets: Above equilibrium price there is a surplus, which pushes price down.
Below equilibrium price there is a shortage, which pushes price up.
An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and quantity; an increase in supply lowers price and raises quantity.
Elasticity measures how strongly quantity responds to price; demand is elastic when the percentage change in quantity exceeds the percentage change in price.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Own price moves you along the curve. Every other determinant shifts the curve. Read the question for which one changed.

content.problem: Given Qd = 15 − 2P and Qs = 5 + 3P, find the equilibrium price and quantity.

steps.operation: Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied
steps.reason: At equilibrium the market clears, so Qd = Qs.
steps.predictPrompt: How do you collect the P terms on one side?

steps.reason: Subtract 5 from both sides and add 2P to both sides.
Either equation gives the equilibrium quantity at P = 2.
steps.result: Qd = 15 − 2(2) = 11, and Qs = 5 + 3(2) = 11. Equilibrium is P = 2, Q = 11.

content.question: The price of petrol rises. Explain why this shifts the demand curve for large cars rather than moving along it.
hints: Petrol is not the price of the car itself; it is the price of a complementary good used with the car.
A change in the price of a complement changes demand at every car price, so the whole curve shifts left.
A strong answer distinguishes the own-price movement from a shift caused by a related good.

lessons.title: Production, Factors and Diminishing Returns
lessons.objective: Match each factor of production to its reward and explain why marginal product eventually falls.

content.heading: Factors of production and their rewards
paragraphs: Production combines four factors of production. Each is paid a reward that reflects its contribution.
bullets: Land — all natural resources; reward is rent.
Labour — human effort, physical and mental; reward is wages or salaries.
Capital — man-made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines and buildings; reward is interest.
Entrepreneurship — organises the other factors and bears risk; reward is profit (which can be negative).
Division of labour splits work into specialised tasks. It raises output per worker but can cause boredom, over-dependence and coordination costs.

content.heading: Diminishing returns and costs
paragraphs: In the short run at least one factor is fixed. Adding more of a variable factor to it eventually yields smaller extra output — the law of diminishing returns.
bullets: Marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of the variable factor.
Diminishing returns sets in when marginal product starts to fall, even though total output may still be rising.
Fixed costs do not change with output (rent, machinery). Variable costs do (raw materials, hourly labour).
Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Marginal product falls before total product does. Total output can keep rising while each extra worker adds less than the one before.

content.problem: A farm has fixed land. With 1, 2, 3 and 4 workers, total output is 10, 25, 35 and 40 tonnes. At which worker do diminishing returns set in?

steps.reason: Marginal product is the change in total output when one more worker is added.
steps.predictPrompt: Which is the first fall in marginal product?

steps.reason: Diminishing returns begin when marginal product turns downward.
steps.result: MP rises from 10 to 15, then falls to 10 at the third worker.

steps.reason: The third worker adds less than the second, so the law has set in.
steps.result: Diminishing returns set in at the third worker, even though total output rises to 35 tonnes.

content.question: A bakery pays N200,000 a month in rent and N5,000 per worker per day. Classify each cost and explain what happens to average fixed cost as output rises.
hints: Rent is paid whether or not bread is baked, so it is fixed. Daily wages vary with the number of workers, so they are variable.
Average fixed cost is fixed cost divided by output.
A strong answer notes that average fixed cost falls as output rises, while average variable cost may fall and then rise.

lessons.title: Market Structures
lessons.objective: Distinguish perfect competition, monopoly, oligopoly and monopolistic competition by sellers, products and entry.

content.heading: Perfect competition
paragraphs: Perfect competition is a benchmark market with many small firms selling an identical product. No single firm can influence the market price.
bullets: Many buyers and many sellers, each too small to affect price.
Homogeneous (identical) products, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
Free entry and exit, and perfect information about prices.
The firm is a price taker: its demand curve is horizontal at the market price.

content.heading: Imperfect markets
paragraphs: When a firm can influence price, the market is imperfect. The three main forms differ by how many firms there are and whether products are differentiated.
bullets: Monopoly: one seller, no close substitute, high barriers to entry; the firm is a price maker.
Oligopoly: a few large firms whose decisions depend on one another; advertising and non-price competition are common.
Monopolistic competition: many firms selling differentiated products, with easy entry.
A monopsony is the mirror image — one buyer facing many sellers.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Ask three questions: how many sellers, is the product identical or differentiated, and can new firms enter? Those three answers identify almost every market structure.

content.problem: A single firm supplies electricity to a city and no other firm can enter the market. Which market structure is this, and why does government usually regulate its price?

steps.reason: One seller is the defining feature of monopoly.
Electricity has no close substitute for most users, and the grid is a natural barrier to entry.
steps.result: The firm can set price without competitive pressure.

steps.reason: A price-making monopolist may restrict output and charge high prices.
steps.result: Government regulates the tariff to protect consumers while allowing the firm to cover costs.

content.question: Why do firms in an oligopoly advertise heavily while perfectly competitive firms do not?
hints: Perfectly competitive firms sell identical products at the market price, so advertising cannot raise their price.
Oligopolists sell differentiated products and compete for market share; advertising can shift demand toward them.
A strong answer links advertising to product differentiation and interdependence.

lessons.title: Money and Inflation
lessons.objective: Name the functions and qualities of money and distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation.

content.heading: Functions and qualities of money
paragraphs: Money is anything generally accepted as a means of payment. It removes the double coincidence of wants that makes barter difficult.
bullets: Functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Qualities: generally acceptable, divisible, portable, durable, homogeneous and limited in supply.
Homogeneity matters because every unit must be identical, so values can be counted and compared.
Anything that fails these qualities — cattle, cowries, cocoa — is a poor money even if it is valuable.

content.heading: Inflation
paragraphs: Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money. Deflation is the opposite.
bullets: Demand-pull inflation: aggregate demand grows faster than output.
Cost-push inflation: rising costs of inputs such as fuel, wages or imported raw materials push prices up.
Imported inflation: higher prices of imported goods enter the domestic price level.
Fixed-income earners, savers and creditors lose purchasing power; borrowers gain because debts are repaid in cheaper money.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Demand-pull starts with buyers; cost-push starts with sellers’ costs. Excess demand over supply is always demand-pull.

content.problem: Government pays a large cash transfer, households spend it quickly, but output is unchanged. Which type of inflation follows, and who loses most?

steps.reason: The extra spending raises aggregate demand, while output has not risen.
steps.result: Demand exceeds supply, so prices are pulled up.
steps.predictPrompt: Does this originate with buyers or with costs?

steps.reason: Inflation caused by excess demand is demand-pull.
People whose incomes are fixed in naira can buy less as prices rise.
steps.result: Fixed-income earners and savers lose the most; borrowers gain.

content.question: A farmer’s diesel, fertiliser and transport costs all rise, and food prices follow. Identify the inflation type and one policy response, noting its limitation.
hints: The increase begins on the cost side, not with excess demand.
A central bank can raise interest rates to reduce demand, but that does not lower fuel or fertiliser costs directly.
A strong answer names cost-push inflation and explains the trade-off between fighting inflation and protecting output.

lessons.title: International Trade and Comparative Advantage
lessons.objective: Explain the gains from trade, compute opportunity cost, and distinguish the terms of trade from the balances.

content.heading: Why countries trade
paragraphs: Countries trade because they differ in resources, technology and costs. Specialising where opportunity cost is lowest raises total output, and both sides can gain.
bullets: Absolute advantage: a country can produce more of a good with the same resources.
Comparative advantage: a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost. This, not absolute advantage, is the basis of beneficial trade.
David Ricardo showed that even a country that is better at everything gains by specialising where its disadvantage is smallest.
Other gains: economies of scale, wider consumer choice and access to goods a country cannot produce.

content.heading: Terms of trade and the balances
paragraphs: The terms of trade measure the rate at which exports exchange for imports. The two balances measure different things and are often confused.
bullets: Terms of trade = (index of export prices ÷ index of import prices) × 100. A rise means exports buy more imports.
Balance of trade = visible exports − visible imports. It covers goods only.
Balance of payments = all receipts and payments, including services, income and transfers. It can balance even when trade does not.
Invisible trade covers services such as banking, shipping, insurance and tourism.
ECOWAS promotes trade and free movement among West African states; its slow progress is often blamed on weak political will and inadequate resources.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A trade deficit is not the same as a payments deficit. Services, remittances and capital inflows can close a goods gap.

content.problem: With the same resources, Country A can produce 10 tonnes of cocoa or 5 tonnes of coffee; Country B can produce 4 tonnes of cocoa or 8 tonnes of coffee. Who should produce which?

steps.reason: Giving up 10 cocoa frees resources for 5 coffee, so 1 coffee costs 2 cocoa.
steps.result: A: 1 coffee = 2 cocoa, or 1 cocoa = 0.5 coffee.
steps.predictPrompt: Now do the same for B.

steps.reason: Giving up 4 cocoa frees resources for 8 coffee, so 1 coffee costs 0.5 cocoa.
steps.result: B: 1 coffee = 0.5 cocoa, or 1 cocoa = 2 coffee.

steps.reason: Each country should produce the good for which it gives up less.
steps.result: A has the lower cocoa cost (0.5 coffee vs 2), so A produces cocoa; B has the lower coffee cost (0.5 cocoa vs 2), so B produces coffee.

content.question: Explain dumping and one reason it harms local producers, then name one trade remedy a government could use.
hints: Dumping is selling exports below home cost or below the price charged at home.
Foreign goods priced below local production cost can take market share and force local firms to cut prices or close.
A government can impose an anti-dumping duty or a tariff to raise the imported price.
